title: More Bhagats ahead
hook: Namdev, Ravidas, Dhanna, Sain and others wait for year three

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gurus answering Farid. Your line was a conversation across centuries. Did you answer someone older with kindness? Today, the last day with the Bhagats for now, and a look at who's still waiting. Day two hundred sixty-three.
screen: `THE GURUS ANSWER FARID — A CONVERSATION ACROSS CENTURIES.`

segments.voice: You know the moment at the end of a good dinner party, when the guests you've been talking to all night start saying goodbye, and you notice, across the room, a whole table of people you never got to meet. Someone's laughing, someone's telling a story, and you think: next time. For twelve days we've sat with two voices, Kabir and Farid. But the Guru's book has a much bigger table. Today, a first glimpse of the others, before we move on. More Bhagats ahead.
screen: `THE END OF A DINNER PARTY.` → `A TABLE YOU NEVER MET.` → `NEXT TIME.`

segments.voice: Let's walk past that table and say the names. Namdev, from Maharashtra, a calico printer, whose hymns are the most numerous after Kabir's; stories say he sang so lovingly that a temple turned toward him. Ravidas of Benares, a leatherworker, from a caste many refused to touch; he sang of Begampura, a city without sorrow, where no one is second-class. Dhanna, a farmer from Rajasthan. Sain, a barber who, it's said, served at a king's court. Pipa, a king who gave up his throne to become a devotee. Trilochan, Beni, Jaidev, Bhikhan, Sadhna, Ramanand, Parmanand, Surdas. Hindus and Muslims, Brahmins and people shut out of temples, across several centuries and much of India. We'll meet them properly later on the path, in year three. For now, notice what twelve days with just two of them showed us. Kabir the weaver, whose loom was a prayer. One light made all. The warrior who fights for the helpless. The death that delights. Short, sharp saloks. Farid of Pakpattan, the first Punjabi voice. Don't strike back. The Creator in creation. Spare the eyes. And the Gurus answering, gently, across the centuries. What they share is what the Gurus heard in them: one God, the Name, love over ritual, and no respect for the walls people build between each other. That's why their words sit in the Guru's book. And it's why the book still has more voices ahead.
screen: `NAMDEV, RAVIDAS, DHANNA, SAIN.` · `PIPA, JAIDEV, SADHNA, SURDAS…` · `TWELVE DAYS WITH KABIR AND FARID.` · `ONE GOD, THE NAME, NO WALLS.` · then, large: `MORE VOICES AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Choose one Bhagat's name from the ones you heard: Namdev, Ravidas, Dhanna, Sain, Pipa, any one. Say it aloud, softly, once. Think of what they were: a printer, a leatherworker, a farmer, a barber, a king. Let that name stand for everyone whose work the world overlooks, and whose voice was still kept. Rest with the breath, and the name. The bell holds the time.
More Bhagats ahead. Namdev, Ravidas, Dhanna, Sain and others, whose hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib and wait for us later on the path.
Your line: more voices ahead. Today, notice one overlooked person, a cleaner, a driver, a quiet colleague, and listen to what they have to say. Day two hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: The hymns of all the Bhagats are read and sung in Sikh worship alongside the Gurus', and communities such as the followers of Ravidas and Namdev especially cherish their hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib.

original.note: Gurmukhi: bhagat bani, the Bhagats' hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kabir and Farid are the only saints in the Granth.
what it means: they're two of fifteen Bhagats, from many castes, regions and faiths, whose hymns sit in the Guru's book.
what a scholar hears: Namdev (c. 13th–14th century, Maharashtra), Ravidas (15th century, Benares) and others; Bhagat bani is arranged by raga with the Gurus' hymns, after them in each section.
